title: Creation
summary: God creates the heavens and the earth, and makes humanity in his image.
dateNote: Placed at the start of the Genesis 5 genealogy; Scripture gives no date.

title: The Fall
summary: Tempted by the serpent, Adam and Eve eat from the tree God forbade them. Sin and death enter the world, and God sends them out of Eden, with the first promise of the serpent's defeat (Genesis 3:15).
dateNote: Scripture doesn't say how long after Creation; placed with it.

title: Cain and Abel
summary: God accepts Abel's offering and not Cain's; Cain kills his brother in anger, and God sends him out to wander, marked so that no one will kill him.
dateNote: Before Seth's birth, when Adam was 130 (Genesis 4:25; 5:3); how long before isn't told.

title: The Flood
summary: God judges a corrupt world by a flood and saves Noah, his family and the animals in the ark, then makes a covenant never to flood the earth again.
dateNote: 1,656 years after Creation by the Masoretic genealogies (Genesis 5; 7:6). The Septuagint and other readings give different totals.

title: The Tower of Babel
summary: People unite to build a tower to the heavens; God confuses their language and scatters them.
dateNote: Sometimes linked to the days of Peleg, because "in his days the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25).

title: Birth of Abram
summary: Abram is born to Terah in Ur of the Chaldeans.
dateNote: Counted back from the Exodus: 430 years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40), Jacob 130 when he went there (Genesis 47:9), Isaac 60 at Jacob's birth (25:26), Abraham 100 at Isaac's (21:5).

title: The call of Abram
summary: At 75, Abram obeys God's call to leave Haran for a land God will show him, with the promise that all nations will be blessed through him.
dateNote: Abram was 75 (Genesis 12:4).

title: Abram in Egypt
summary: A famine drives Abram to Egypt, where he passes Sarai off as his sister and God protects her.
dateNote: Soon after the call; Scripture doesn't say how soon.

title: Abram and Lot part ways
summary: Their herds grow too large to share the land; Lot chooses the Jordan plain near Sodom and Abram settles at Hebron.
dateNote: After the return from Egypt; the year is an estimate.

title: Abram and Melchizedek
summary: Abram rescues Lot from four invading kings, pursuing them as far as Dan. On his return Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything.
dateNote: After Lot moved to Sodom and before God's covenant with Abram, which came "after these events" (Genesis 15:1); the year is an estimate. Salem is usually taken to be Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2).

title: God's covenant with Abram
summary: God promises Abram offspring as many as the stars and confirms the promise of the land with a covenant ceremony.
dateNote: Before Ishmael's birth, within Abram's first ten years in Canaan (Genesis 16:3); the year is an estimate.

title: Birth of Ishmael
summary: Hagar bears Abram a son, Ishmael, after God meets her in the wilderness.
dateNote: Abram was 86 (Genesis 16:16).

title: Covenant of circumcision
summary: God renames Abram as Abraham and Sarai as Sarah, gives circumcision as the covenant sign, and promises a son within a year.
dateNote: Abraham was 99 (Genesis 17:1).

title: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
summary: Three visitors come to Abraham's tent at Mamre and promise that Sarah will have a son: "Is anything too difficult for the LORD?" Then Abraham pleads for Sodom, and God rescues Lot and destroys Sodom and Gomorrah.
dateNote: The same year as the covenant of circumcision, a year before Isaac's birth (Genesis 18:10).

title: Birth of Isaac
summary: Sarah bears Isaac when Abraham is 100, just as God promised. When Isaac is weaned, Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, and in the wilderness God hears the boy's cry and saves them.
dateNote: Abraham was 100 (Genesis 21:5).

title: Abraham offers Isaac
summary: God tests Abraham by asking him to sacrifice Isaac on Mount Moriah, then provides a ram in his place.
dateNote: Isaac's age is not given; the date is an estimate.

title: Death of Sarah
summary: Sarah dies at 127; Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah, his first owned land in Canaan, to bury her.
dateNote: Sarah was 127 (Genesis 23:1), ten years younger than Abraham (17:17).

title: Isaac marries Rebekah
summary: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah among Abraham's relatives near Haran, and she becomes Isaac's wife.
dateNote: Isaac was 40 (Genesis 25:20).

title: Birth of Jacob and Esau
summary: Rebekah bears twins; God says the older will serve the younger. Grown, Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew: "Thus Esau despised his birthright."
dateNote: Isaac was 60 (Genesis 25:26).

title: Job's trials
summary: Job, a blameless man of Uz, loses his wealth, his children and his health. His friends insist he must have sinned; Job protests his innocence and demands an answer, until God speaks out of the whirlwind.
dateNote: Not dated, and Uz can't be located. The setting looks like the patriarchs' time: wealth counted in flocks, Job offering sacrifice for his family as its head, no mention of Israel or the Law, and a life of over 140 years (Job 42:16). When the book was written is unknown.

title: Death of Abraham
summary: Abraham dies at 175 and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael beside Sarah.
dateNote: Abraham was 175 (Genesis 25:7).

title: Jacob flees to Haran
summary: After taking Esau's blessing, Jacob flees to Laban and dreams of a stairway to heaven at Bethel.
dateNote: Estimated from Jacob's age at the move to Egypt and his years with Laban.

title: Jacob marries Leah and Rachel
summary: Jacob works fourteen years for Laban's daughters; his sons, the ancestors of Israel's tribes, are born in Haran.
dateNote: Jacob served seven years for Rachel, was given Leah, and served seven more (Genesis 29:20–30); his sons were born in those years.

title: Jacob returns to Canaan
summary: After twenty years with Laban, Jacob brings his family home: past Esau at Peniel, through Shechem and Bethel, to Isaac at Hebron.
dateNote: Twenty years after he fled (Genesis 31:38, 41). How long the journey took isn't told.

title: Jacob wrestles with God
summary: Returning to Canaan, Jacob wrestles with God at Peniel, is renamed Israel, and is reconciled with Esau.
dateNote: On the way home, twenty years after Jacob fled (Genesis 31:41).

title: Joseph sold into slavery
summary: Jealous of their father's favorite, Joseph's brothers sell him to traders bound for Egypt.
dateNote: Joseph was 17 (Genesis 37:2).

title: Joseph in prison
summary: Joseph serves in Potiphar's house, and "the LORD was with Joseph." He refuses the advances of Potiphar's wife, is falsely accused and thrown into prison, and there interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker: "Don't interpretations belong to God?"
dateNote: From when he was sold, at 17 (Genesis 37:2), to when he stood before Pharaoh, at 30 (Genesis 41:46).

title: Joseph rules in Egypt
summary: Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams and is made second in command to prepare Egypt for seven years of famine.
dateNote: Joseph was 30 (Genesis 41:46).

title: Death of Isaac
summary: Isaac dies at 180 and is buried by Esau and Jacob.
dateNote: Isaac was 180 (Genesis 35:28).

title: Joseph's brothers come to Egypt
summary: Famine drives Jacob's sons to Egypt for grain, and they bow before Joseph without knowing him. He tests them, keeping Simeon and demanding Benjamin, until Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place. Then Joseph tells them, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" and "it was to save lives that God sent me before you."
dateNote: Two years into the famine (Genesis 45:6), the year Jacob moved to Egypt; the brothers' first trip may have been a year earlier.

title: Jacob's family moves to Egypt
summary: Pharaoh invites Joseph's family to Egypt. On the way God tells Jacob not to be afraid, and his household of seventy settles in Goshen.
dateNote: Jacob was 130 (Genesis 47:9), 430 years before the Exodus (Exodus 12:40).

title: Death of Jacob
summary: Jacob blesses Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh, then his own twelve sons, and dies at 147; Joseph carries him back to be buried at Machpelah.
dateNote: Jacob was 147 (Genesis 47:28).

title: Death of Joseph
summary: Joseph dies at 110, making Israel promise to carry his bones to the Promised Land.
dateNote: Joseph was 110 (Genesis 50:26).

title: Hammurabi's laws
summary: Hammurabi of Babylon sets up stone pillars carved with nearly 300 laws, among the oldest law codes known. Readers often compare them with the Law given at Sinai: some laws are alike, but the Law of Moses is a covenant with God.
dateNote: About 1754 BC. The best-known copy, found at Susa in 1901, is in the Louvre.

title: Israel enslaved in Egypt
summary: A new king who did not know Joseph forces the growing Israelite people into hard labor building store cities.
dateNote: Scripture does not date the start of the oppression; these spans are estimates.

title: Egypt drives out the Hyksos
summary: Pharaoh Ahmose drives the Hyksos kings out of the Nile Delta and founds Egypt's New Kingdom.
dateNote: About 1550 BC. Some readers link "a new king, who did not know Joseph" (Exodus 1:8) with the change of rulers here.

title: Birth of Moses
summary: Hidden from Pharaoh's decree, the infant Moses is found in the Nile by Pharaoh's daughter and raised in the palace.
dateNote: Moses was 80 when he and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7).

title: Moses flees to Midian
summary: After killing an Egyptian, Moses flees to Midian, marries Zipporah and tends Jethro's flocks for forty years.
dateNote: Moses was 40 (Acts 7:23).

title: The burning bush
summary: God appears to Moses in a bush that does not burn up, reveals his name, and sends him to bring Israel out of Egypt.
dateNote: Forty years after Moses fled to Midian (Acts 7:30), shortly before the Exodus.

title: The ten plagues
summary: Pharaoh refuses to let Israel go and makes them gather their own straw for bricks. God strikes Egypt with ten plagues.
dateNote: Scripture doesn't say how long the plagues lasted; they end with the Passover on the 14th of the first month (Exodus 12:6).

title: The first Passover
summary: Israel marks its doorposts with the blood of a lamb, and the Lord passes over them when he strikes the firstborn of Egypt.
dateNote: The 14th day of the first month (Exodus 12:2, 6). Nisan falls in March–April.

title: The Exodus
summary: God brings Israel out of Egypt, leading them by a pillar of cloud and fire from Rameses through the sea to Mount Sinai.
description: Israel sets out from Rameses the day after Passover, about 600,000 men plus women and children (Exodus 12:37). God leads them not by the coastal road but through the wilderness toward the sea, where he parts the waters and destroys Pharaoh's army. They travel on through Marah, Elim and the wilderness of Sin, arriving at Mount Sinai in the third month.
dateNote: Early date (c. 1446 BC): 480 years before Solomon began the temple (1 Kings 6:1). Late date (c. 1260 BC): fits the city name Rameses (Exodus 1:11) and the reign of Rameses II.

title: Crossing the Red Sea
summary: God parts the sea, Israel crosses on dry ground, and the waters return over Pharaoh's chariots. Moses and Miriam lead a song of praise.
dateNote: A few days after Israel left Rameses on the 15th of the first month (Numbers 33:3–8); Scripture doesn't give the day.

title: Manna and quail
summary: When Israel grumbles for food, God sends quail in the evening and bread from heaven each morning.
dateNote: Exodus 16:1.

title: Battle with Amalek
summary: At Rephidim God gives water from the rock; Joshua defeats Amalek while Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' hands.
dateNote: At Rephidim, between the wilderness of Sin in the 2nd month and Sinai in the 3rd (Exodus 16:1; 17:1; 19:1).

title: The Ten Commandments
summary: At Mount Sinai God gives the Ten Commandments and makes his covenant with Israel as his treasured people.
dateNote: Israel arrived "in the third month" after leaving Egypt (Exodus 19:1).

title: The golden calf
summary: While Moses is on the mountain, the people make a golden calf; Moses intercedes and God renews the covenant.
dateNote: About forty days after Moses went up the mountain (Exodus 24:18).

title: The tabernacle is set up
summary: On the mountain God shows Moses the pattern for the tabernacle, and the people bring gifts and build it. On the first day of the second year it is raised, and the glory of the Lord fills it.
dateNote: The first day of the first month of the second year (Exodus 40:17).

title: Laws for worship and holiness
summary: From the tabernacle God gives Moses the laws of the offerings, Aaron and his sons are ordained as priests, and the yearly Day of Atonement is set. "Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy," and "love your neighbor as yourself."
dateNote: Spoken from the newly raised tabernacle (Leviticus 1:1), before the census on the first day of the second month (Numbers 1:1).

title: Israel leaves Sinai
summary: Israel is counted and camped by tribes. Then the cloud lifts from the tabernacle and they set out toward the Promised Land. On the way they crave meat and God sends quail, and Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses.
dateNote: Numbers 10:11.

title: The twelve spies
summary: Ten spies bring a fearful report; only Joshua and Caleb trust God. Israel refuses to enter and is sentenced to forty years in the wilderness.
dateNote: "It was the season for the first ripe grapes" (Numbers 13:20), in summer.

title: Forty years in the wilderness
summary: The generation that refused to enter the land dies in the wilderness while God continues to provide for his people.
dateNote: From the sentence that follows the spies' report (Numbers 14:33–34), forty years counted from the Exodus.

title: Korah's rebellion
summary: Korah, Dathan and Abiram lead 250 leaders of Israel against Moses and Aaron. "The ground beneath them split open" and swallowed the rebels. To show whom God has chosen as priest, Aaron's staff sprouts, blossoms and produces almonds overnight.
dateNote: Scripture doesn't date it; Numbers tells it after the spies, in the years of wandering.

title: Death of Miriam
summary: Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh.
dateNote: "In the first month" (Numbers 20:1); the 40th year, since Aaron died later that year (Numbers 33:38).

title: Moses strikes the rock
summary: At Kadesh the people have no water. God tells Moses to speak to the rock, but Moses strikes it twice. Water gushes out, but the LORD tells Moses and Aaron: "Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them."
dateNote: At Kadesh after Miriam's death (Numbers 20:1–2).

title: Death of Aaron
summary: Aaron dies on Mount Hor at 123, and his son Eleazar becomes high priest.
dateNote: Numbers 33:38.

title: The bronze serpent
summary: On the long way around Edom the people speak against God and Moses, and venomous snakes bite them. Moses makes a bronze snake and mounts it on a pole: anyone bitten who looks at it lives. Jesus says, "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up" (John 3:14).
dateNote: After Aaron's death in the 5th month and before Israel reached the plains of Moab (Numbers 21:4; 22:1); Scripture gives no date.

title: Journey to the Plains of Moab
summary: Israel travels around Edom, defeats Sihon and Og, and camps on the plains of Moab across from Jericho.
dateNote: From Kadesh in the first month of the 40th year (Numbers 20:1) to the plains of Moab, where Moses spoke in the 11th month (Deuteronomy 1:3–5).

title: Balaam and his donkey
summary: Balak king of Moab hires the seer Balaam to curse Israel. On the way an angel blocks the road and Balaam's donkey speaks. From the heights over Israel's camp Balaam can only bless: "How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?" He sees a star that "will come forth from Jacob."
dateNote: While Israel camped on the plains of Moab (Numbers 22:1), before Moses' last words in the 11th month of the 40th year (Deuteronomy 1:3).

title: Moses' farewell to Israel
summary: On the plains of Moab Moses lays hands on Joshua as his successor and retells the Law to the generation about to enter the land: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength." He sets before them "life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life."
dateNote: Deuteronomy 1:3–5.

title: Death of Moses
summary: After giving his final words to Israel, Moses views the Promised Land from Mount Nebo and dies at 120. Joshua succeeds him.
dateNote: Moses spoke Deuteronomy in the 11th month of the 40th year (Deuteronomy 1:3).

title: Conquest of Canaan
summary: Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan and through campaigns in the center, south and north of Canaan, breaking the power of its kings.
dateNote: About seven years: Caleb was 40 when sent as a spy and 85 when the land was divided (Joshua 14:7–10).

title: Rahab hides the spies
summary: Joshua sends two spies to Jericho. Rahab hides them on her roof, telling them "the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below," and lets them down by a rope through her window. They swear to spare her family when the city falls.
dateNote: A few days before the crossing on the 10th of the first month (Joshua 2:22; 3:2; 4:19).

title: Crossing the Jordan
summary: The Jordan stops flowing when the priests carrying the ark step into it, and Israel crosses into the Promised Land on dry ground.
dateNote: Joshua 4:19, forty years after the Exodus.

title: The fall of Jericho
summary: Israel marches around Jericho for seven days; at the trumpet blast and shout its walls fall. Rahab and her family are spared.
dateNote: After the Passover at Gilgal on the 14th of the first month (Joshua 5:10) and seven days of marching around the city.

title: The sun stands still at Gibeon
summary: Joshua defends Gibeon against five Amorite kings, and the sun stands still until Israel has won.
dateNote: In the southern campaign, early in the conquest; Scripture gives no date.

title: The land divided among the tribes
summary: Joshua divides the land among the tribes by lot, and the tabernacle is set up at Shiloh.
dateNote: Caleb is 85, forty-five years after the spies (Joshua 14:7–10).

title: Joshua renews the covenant
summary: Near the end of his life Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem: "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" He dies at 110.
dateNote: Near the end of Joshua's life, "a long time" after the conquest (Joshua 23:1); he died at 110 (Joshua 24:29). His birth year is estimated, so this date is too.

title: Israel without a king
summary: Micah of Ephraim sets up a shrine with an idol, and the tribe of Dan carries it off when it seizes a new home in the north. A Levite's concubine is abused and killed at Gibeah, and the tribes nearly wipe out Benjamin in the war that follows. "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."
dateNote: Told at the end of Judges but set early in it: Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, is still priest (Judges 20:28), and Moses' grandson Jonathan serves Dan's idols (Judges 18:30). Dates in Judges are approximate: the book's periods of oppression and rest add up to more than the time available, so some probably overlapped.

title: Othniel and Ehud
summary: After Joshua's generation, "another generation rose up who did not know the LORD." Israel serves the Baals and falls to its enemies, then cries out, and God raises up judges: first Othniel, Caleb's nephew, then Ehud, "a left-handed Benjamite," who kills Eglon king of Moab and sets Israel free.
dateNote: Eight years under Cushan-rishathaim and forty of rest under Othniel come before Moab's eighteen (Judges 3:8–14). Dates in Judges are approximate: the book's periods of oppression and rest add up to more than the time available, so some probably overlapped.

title: Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera
summary: At Deborah's word Barak leads ten thousand men from Mount Tabor; the Kishon sweeps away Sisera's chariots, and Jael kills Sisera.
dateNote: Dates in Judges are approximate: the book's periods of oppression and rest add up to more than the time available, so some probably overlapped.

title: The Sea Peoples and the Bronze Age collapse
summary: Raiders from the Aegean sweep the eastern Mediterranean as the Hittite Empire and many cities fall. Ramesses III drives them back from Egypt, and one of their peoples, the Philistines, settles the coast of Canaan.
dateNote: Ramesses III's victory, carved on his temple at Medinet Habu, is dated about 1177 BC; the collapse took decades.

title: Gideon defeats Midian
summary: God sends Gideon against the Midianite raiders with just three hundred men, armed with trumpets, jars and torches. After his death his son Abimelech kills his brothers and makes himself king at Shechem, until a woman drops a millstone on his head.
dateNote: Dates in Judges are approximate: the book's periods of oppression and rest add up to more than the time available, so some probably overlapped.

title: Ruth and Boaz
summary: Ruth the Moabite returns with Naomi to Bethlehem, gleans in Boaz's field, and marries him. Their son Obed is David's grandfather.
dateNote: Set "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). Boaz is David's great-grandfather, which points to the late 1100s BC.

title: Birth of Samuel
summary: Hannah prays at Shiloh for a son; when Samuel is born she gives him to serve the Lord under Eli.
dateNote: Estimated: Samuel was old by the time Israel asked for a king (1 Samuel 8:1).

title: God calls Samuel
summary: At Shiloh, when "the word of the LORD was rare," God calls the boy Samuel by name in the night. Samuel answers, "Speak, for Your servant is listening," and hears of the judgment coming on Eli's house. All Israel comes to know him as a prophet.
dateNote: Samuel is still a boy (1 Samuel 3:1); Josephus says he was twelve.

title: Jephthah's vow
summary: Driven out by his brothers, Jephthah of Gilead is called back to lead Israel against the Ammonites. He vows that "whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me" on his return will be the LORD's, as a burnt offering, and his only daughter comes out to meet him.
dateNote: Jephthah tells the Ammonites Israel has held the land east of the Jordan for "three hundred years" (Judges 11:26), which fits the early date of the Exodus; late-daters take it as a round number. Dates in Judges are approximate: the book's periods of oppression and rest add up to more than the time available, so some probably overlapped.

title: Samson fights the Philistines
summary: Samson, set apart from birth, fights the Philistines alone for twenty years, until Delilah betrays him; he dies pulling down the temple of Dagon at Gaza.
dateNote: He judged Israel twenty years (Judges 16:31), during the Philistine oppression that runs into Samuel's day. Dates in Judges are approximate: the book's periods of oppression and rest add up to more than the time available, so some probably overlapped.

title: The ark captured
summary: The Philistines defeat Israel at Aphek and capture the ark of the covenant. Eli's sons die in battle and Eli dies at the news. Twenty years later Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah, the Philistines are routed, and he sets up a stone, Ebenezer: "Thus far the LORD has helped us."
dateNote: The ark then stays twenty years at Kiriath-jearim before Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:2).

title: Saul becomes king
summary: Israel asks Samuel for a king like the other nations. God gives them Saul, whom Samuel anoints and the people acclaim.
dateNote: Acts 13:21 gives Saul forty years; the numbers in 1 Samuel 13:1 are damaged in the Hebrew text.

title: Saul is rejected
summary: Saul offers the sacrifice at Gilgal rather than wait for Samuel. At Michmash Jonathan and his armor-bearer rout a Philistine garrison. Later Saul spares Agag king of Amalek and the best of the plunder, and Samuel tells him, "obedience is better than sacrifice": the LORD has rejected him as king.
dateNote: Not dated; before Samuel anoints David (1 Samuel 16:1).

title: Samuel anoints David
summary: God rejects Saul and sends Samuel to Bethlehem, where he anoints Jesse's youngest son, the shepherd David.
dateNote: Not dated in Scripture; David is the youngest son, still keeping the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11).

title: David and Goliath
summary: The young David faces the Philistine champion Goliath with a sling and five stones, trusting the Lord, and kills him.
dateNote: Not dated in Scripture; David is still a youth (1 Samuel 17:33).

title: David flees from Saul
summary: Jonathan loves David "as himself," but Saul's jealousy turns murderous, and David flees. Hunted through the wilderness, he twice spares Saul's life: "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD's anointed." He marries Abigail, and at last takes refuge among the Philistines at Ziklag.
dateNote: From soon after David killed Goliath until Saul's death, when David was 30 (2 Samuel 5:4); his last year and four months were spent in Philistine territory (1 Samuel 27:7).

title: Death of Saul and Jonathan
summary: The night before the battle Saul consults a medium at Endor. The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan is killed and the wounded Saul falls on his own sword.
dateNote: Counted back from the kingdom's division in 931 BC: David reigned forty years after Saul (2 Samuel 5:4).

title: David's reign
summary: David rules seven and a half years from Hebron over Judah, then thirty-three years from Jerusalem over all Israel.
dateNote: Forty years in all (2 Samuel 5:4–5).

title: David takes Jerusalem
summary: David captures the Jebusite stronghold of Zion and makes Jerusalem his capital, then brings the ark there.
dateNote: After seven and a half years reigning in Hebron (2 Samuel 5:5).

title: God's covenant with David
summary: Through Nathan, God promises David a house and a kingdom that will last forever: a promise the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus.
dateNote: Not dated; it comes once David is settled in his palace in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 7:1).

title: David and Bathsheba
summary: David takes Bathsheba and has her husband Uriah killed. Nathan confronts him, and David repents (Psalm 51), but trouble follows his house.
dateNote: Not dated; it happens while Israel's army besieges Rabbah of the Ammonites (2 Samuel 11:1).

title: Absalom's rebellion
summary: Absalom kills his brother Amnon, who had raped their sister Tamar. Later he wins the people's hearts and has himself proclaimed king at Hebron, and David flees Jerusalem. In the battle that follows, Absalom's head is caught in an oak and he is killed. David weeps: "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom!"
dateNote: Not dated; some years after David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 13:23, 38; 14:28; 15:7).

title: David's psalms
summary: David, "the sweet psalmist of Israel," writes songs of lament, trust and praise. About half of the 150 psalms bear his name, among them Psalm 23 and his prayer of repentance, Psalm 51.
dateNote: Through his life; some, like Psalms 57 and 59, from before his reign, while he fled from Saul. Most of Psalms 1–72 are his, ending "Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse" (Psalm 72:20), though psalms of the sons of Korah and Asaph are among them; more of his are in the later books (Psalms 101–145). The whole book grew over centuries, from Moses (Psalm 90) to the exile (Psalm 137).

title: Solomon's reign
summary: Solomon asks God for wisdom, rules Israel at the height of its wealth and peace, and builds the temple, but his many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods.
dateNote: Forty years (1 Kings 11:42).

title: Solomon asks for wisdom
summary: At Gibeon God appears to Solomon in a dream: "Ask, and I will give it to you!" Solomon asks for "an understanding heart to judge Your people." Back in Jerusalem two women claim the same baby, and Solomon's order to cut it in two shows which is the mother.
dateNote: Early in his reign, before the temple was begun in his fourth year (1 Kings 3:1–4; 6:1).

title: Solomon builds the temple
summary: Solomon builds the house of the Lord on Mount Moriah; at its dedication God's glory fills the temple.
dateNote: Begun in Solomon's fourth year, 480 years after the Exodus (1 Kings 6:1), and finished seven years later (1 Kings 6:37–38).

title: Solomon's wisdom
summary: God gives Solomon wisdom beyond all others: he speaks three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs. The queen of Sheba comes to test him with hard questions. Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs bear his name.
dateNote: Through his reign (1 Kings 4:29–34). Proverbs also gathers sayings of others, and some of Solomon's were copied out by Hezekiah's men about 700 BC (Proverbs 25:1). Ecclesiastes is traditionally Solomon's, from late in life; many date it later.

title: The kingdom divides
summary: When Rehoboam refuses to lighten Solomon's heavy demands, the ten northern tribes make Jeroboam king. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and a man of God from Judah cries out against his altar. In Rehoboam's fifth year Shishak of Egypt plunders Jerusalem and carries off the temple's treasures.
dateNote: 931 BC in Thiele's chronology of the kings, counted from the reigns given in Kings. Shishak's raid (1 Kings 14:25) is the campaign Pharaoh Shoshenq I listed on a temple wall at Karnak, about 925 BC.

title: Omri builds Samaria
summary: For fifty years after the division, Israel and Judah are at war. In Judah, Asa removes the idols and trusts God against a vast army from Cush. In Israel, king after king is murdered, until the army commander Omri takes the throne and builds a new capital on the hill of Samaria.
dateNote: Omri reigned twelve years, the first six at Tirzah (1 Kings 16:23–24); in Thiele's chronology he moved to Samaria about 880 BC. Assyrian records long afterward called Israel "the house of Omri."

title: Elijah on Mount Carmel
summary: Elijah tells King Ahab, who serves Baal with his queen Jezebel, that no rain will fall. Fed by ravens and then by a widow at Zarephath, whose son he raises from the dead, he waits out three years of drought. Then on Mount Carmel he challenges the prophets of Baal: "How long will you waver between two opinions?" God answers with fire from heaven, and the rain returns.
dateNote: During Ahab's reign (874–853 BC); the year isn't given.

title: Elijah at Horeb
summary: When Jezebel vows to kill him, Elijah flees past Beersheba and asks to die. An angel feeds him, and he walks forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God. There the LORD is not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire: "after the fire came a still, small voice." God sends him back to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place.
dateNote: Right after Carmel, when Jezebel hears what Elijah has done (1 Kings 19:1–3).

title: Naboth's vineyard
summary: Naboth will not sell Ahab the vineyard beside his palace in Jezreel, his family's inheritance, so Jezebel has him falsely accused and stoned. Elijah meets Ahab in the vineyard: "Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?" Where the dogs licked Naboth's blood, they will lick his. Ahab humbles himself, and the disaster is put off to his son's days.
dateNote: Not dated; late in Ahab's reign (874–853 BC), before his death, which Elijah's word foretells (1 Kings 22:38).

title: The battle of Qarqar
summary: Ahab of Israel joins a coalition of kings, with 2,000 chariots, to stop Shalmaneser III of Assyria in Syria: the first time a king of Israel appears in another nation's records.
dateNote: 853 BC, recorded on Shalmaneser's Kurkh Monolith; Scripture doesn't mention it. Qarqar was on the Orontes in Syria.

title: Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead
summary: Ahab twice defeats Ben-hadad of Aram, then lets him go. Three years later he and Jehoshaphat of Judah march on Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets promise victory, but Micaiah says, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd." Ahab goes into battle in disguise, and an arrow shot at random kills him. In Judah, Jehoshaphat sends teachers of the Law through the land, and when Moab and Ammon invade, he is told, "the battle does not belong to you, but to God."
dateNote: Ahab fought Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC (Shalmaneser III's inscription names him) and died later that year, Thiele's date. Jehoshaphat's reforms and wars (2 Chronicles 17–20) aren't dated within his reign.

title: Elijah taken up to heaven
summary: When King Ahaziah of Israel sends to ask the god of Ekron whether he will recover, Elijah tells him he will die. Then Elijah parts the Jordan and is taken up in a whirlwind as chariots of fire appear. Elisha takes up his cloak and his ministry.
dateNote: Not dated; Elisha is already prophet while Jehoshaphat still reigns in Judah (2 Kings 3), before about 848 BC.

title: Elisha's ministry
summary: With a double portion of Elijah's spirit, Elisha heals Jericho's spring, fills a widow's jars with oil, raises the Shunammite woman's son, and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves. Naaman, the Aramean commander, dips in the Jordan seven times and is healed of leprosy. When Aram's army surrounds Dothan, Elisha's servant sees that "the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire." Even after his death, a dead man thrown into his tomb comes back to life.
dateNote: From Elijah's ascension, about 850 BC, to Elisha's death under Jehoash of Israel (2 Kings 13:14–20), who reigned 798–782 BC; the end is estimated.

title: Jehu's revolt
summary: Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint the army commander Jehu king of Israel. Jehu races to Jezreel, "driving like a madman," and kills both King Joram of Israel and King Ahaziah of Judah. Jezebel is thrown from a window, and Jehu wipes out Ahab's family and the worshipers of Baal, yet keeps Jeroboam's golden calves.
dateNote: 841 BC in Thiele's chronology. Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk shows Jehu bowing before him with tribute that year.

title: Joash, the boy king
summary: When Ahaziah dies, his mother Athaliah kills the royal family and seizes Judah's throne. Only the baby Joash is saved, hidden in the temple for six years. Then the priest Jehoiada crowns him and Athaliah is put to death. Joash repairs the temple, but after Jehoiada dies he turns from God and has Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the temple courtyard.
dateNote: Joash was seven when he became king (2 Kings 11:21), in 835 BC in Thiele's chronology.

title: Jonah preaches to Nineveh
summary: Jonah runs from God's call, is swallowed by a great fish, and finally warns Nineveh, which repents and is spared.
dateNote: Jonah prophesied under Jeroboam II of Israel (793–753 BC, 2 Kings 14:25); the year of his mission isn't given.

title: Amos warns Israel
summary: A shepherd from Judah denounces the northern kingdom's injustice and hollow worship at Bethel, and foretells its fall.
dateNote: "Two years before the earthquake," under Uzziah and Jeroboam II (Amos 1:1), about 760 BC.

title: Hosea's ministry
summary: Hosea marries Gomer, who leaves him for other lovers, and takes her back: a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness and God's love. He warns the northern kingdom of judgment in its last decades.
dateNote: In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel (Hosea 1:1): from before 753 BC, when Jeroboam died, into Hezekiah's reign, from 715 BC.

title: Rome founded, by tradition
summary: Roman legend tells that Romulus founds the city on the Tiber that will one day rule Judea.
dateNote: The traditional date, 753 BC, comes from later Roman writers; the site was settled earlier.

title: Isaiah's ministry
summary: Called in a vision of God's holiness, Isaiah counsels Judah's kings, warns of judgment and promises a coming king and a suffering servant.
dateNote: From the year King Uzziah died, about 740 BC (Isaiah 6:1), into Hezekiah's reign and perhaps beyond: Isaiah records Sennacherib's death in 681 BC (Isaiah 37:38). Many scholars assign chapters 40–66, addressed to the exiles, to later prophets of Isaiah's school, during and after the exile.

title: Micah's ministry
summary: A prophet from the Judean countryside condemns the rich who seize fields and the leaders who sell justice, foretells the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem, and names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a coming ruler.
dateNote: In the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1): before Samaria fell in 722 BC, which he foretells (Micah 1:6), and into Hezekiah's reign (Jeremiah 26:18). About 735–700 BC.

title: Ahaz and the sign of Immanuel
summary: Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel march on Jerusalem. Isaiah tells King Ahaz to stand firm and gives him a sign: "Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel." Ahaz instead pays Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, who takes Damascus and carries off Galilee's people, and copies an Assyrian altar for the temple.
dateNote: The war of Aram and Israel against Judah, about 735–732 BC; Tiglath-pileser III's own records list Ahaz among the kings paying him tribute, and his campaigns took Galilee and Damascus in 733–732 BC.

title: Fall of Samaria
summary: After a three-year siege Assyria takes Samaria and deports the people of the northern kingdom. Israel's ten tribes are scattered.
dateNote: Assyrian records credit the conquest to Shalmaneser V and Sargon II; Thiele dates it 723/722 BC.

title: Hezekiah's reform
summary: Hezekiah reopens and cleanses the temple, tears down the high places, and breaks up the bronze serpent Moses had made, to which Israel had been burning incense. He invites all Israel, even the remnant of the north, to keep the Passover in Jerusalem: "nothing like this had happened there since the days of Solomon."
dateNote: In the first month of Hezekiah's first year (2 Chronicles 29:3), 715 BC in Thiele's chronology, which has him reigning alongside Ahaz from 729 BC.

title: Sennacherib threatens Jerusalem
summary: Assyria's king takes Lachish and surrounds Jerusalem. Hezekiah prays, Isaiah promises deliverance, and the angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian camp.
dateNote: Sennacherib's own annals and the reliefs of Lachish from his palace record this campaign of 701 BC.

title: Hezekiah's illness
summary: Hezekiah falls ill and Isaiah tells him he will die. He weeps and prays, and God answers, "I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears," adding fifteen years to his life; as a sign the shadow on Ahaz's stairway goes back ten steps. Afterward he shows envoys from Babylon all his treasures, and Isaiah foretells that everything will be carried off to Babylon.
dateNote: Hezekiah died in 686 BC, fifteen years later (2 Kings 20:6), so about 701 BC, around the time of Sennacherib's invasion.

title: Manasseh's reign
summary: Hezekiah's son rebuilds the high places, sets up altars to the stars in the temple courts, sacrifices his son in the fire, and "shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end." For his sins God declares that Jerusalem will fall. Chronicles adds that the Assyrians took him to Babylon in chains, where he humbled himself, and God brought him back.
dateNote: Fifty-five years (2 Kings 21:1), Judah's longest reign: 697–642 BC in Thiele's chronology, which counts ten years alongside Hezekiah. When he was taken to Babylon isn't known.

title: Zephaniah's warning
summary: Zephaniah warns Judah and the nations of the coming day of the Lord, and promises a humble remnant that God will rejoice over with singing.
dateNote: In the days of Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1). The idol worship he condemns suggests before Josiah's reform of 622 BC, about 630 BC.

title: Nahum foretells Nineveh's fall
summary: A century after Jonah, Nahum announces that Nineveh, Assyria's capital, will fall for its cruelty: comfort for Judah, long under Assyria's yoke.
dateNote: Nahum speaks of the fall of Thebes (663 BC) as past (Nahum 3:8) and Nineveh's (612 BC) as still to come; often placed about 650 BC.

title: Josiah's reform
summary: The Book of the Law is found in the temple. Josiah renews the covenant, destroys the idols and celebrates the Passover.
dateNote: In Josiah's eighteenth year (2 Kings 22:3).

title: Jeremiah's ministry
summary: For four decades Jeremiah warns Judah to repent and submit to Babylon, weeps over Jerusalem's fall, and promises a new covenant.
dateNote: From Josiah's thirteenth year (Jeremiah 1:2) until after Jerusalem fell, when he was taken to Egypt (Jeremiah 43). The end date is estimated.

title: Nineveh falls
summary: Babylonians and Medes take and destroy Nineveh, Assyria's capital, as Nahum had foretold. Within a few years the Assyrian Empire is gone.
dateNote: 612 BC, recorded in the Babylonian Chronicles.

title: Habakkuk questions God
summary: Habakkuk asks why God lets injustice go unpunished, and is told that Babylon is coming. He learns that the righteous will live by faith, and ends in praise though the fig tree fails.
dateNote: Not dated. God is "raising up the Chaldeans" (Habakkuk 1:6), so usually placed just before Babylon's victory at Carchemish in 605 BC.

title: Daniel taken to Babylon
summary: Nebuchadnezzar takes young nobles from Jerusalem to serve in his court, among them Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, whom he renames Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. They refuse the king's food and grow healthier than all the rest.
dateNote: In the third year of Jehoiakim (Daniel 1:1), when Nebuchadnezzar first took Jerusalem in 605 BC.

title: Nebuchadnezzar's dream
summary: Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men tell him both his dream and its meaning. God reveals it to Daniel: a great statue of gold, silver, bronze and iron, smashed by a stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth. The kingdoms of the world will pass, and "the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed."
dateNote: In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign (Daniel 2:1), about 603 BC.

title: The fiery furnace
summary: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue: God can deliver them, "But even if He does not," they will not worship it. They are thrown into the blazing furnace, and the king sees "four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire."
dateNote: Scripture doesn't date it; it's placed after the dream that comes before it in Daniel. The Greek Old Testament dates it to Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year, 587 BC.

title: King Jehoiachin taken to Babylon
summary: Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem, carries King Jehoiachin and ten thousand leading citizens to Babylon, among them the priest Ezekiel, and makes Zedekiah king.
dateNote: The Babylonian Chronicle dates the city's capture to 2 Adar (16 March 597 BC).

title: Fall of Jerusalem
summary: Babylon besieges Jerusalem for a year and a half, breaks through the walls, burns the temple and takes the people into exile.
dateNote: From the start of the siege (2 Kings 25:1) to the burning of the temple (Jeremiah 52:12). Thiele dates the fall to 586 BC; others to 587.

title: Obadiah against Edom
summary: Obadiah condemns Edom, Jacob's brother nation, for gloating and looting as Jerusalem fell, and promises that the kingdom will be the Lord's.
dateNote: Not dated. Edom's part as Jerusalem was plundered (Obadiah 11–14) best fits Babylon's capture of the city in 586 BC (Psalm 137:7). Some link it to a raid under Jehoram of Judah, about 845 BC (2 Chronicles 21:16–17).

title: Ezekiel's ministry
summary: Among the exiles in Babylonia, Ezekiel sees God's glory, warns that Jerusalem will fall, and after it falls promises new hearts, dry bones brought to life, and a new temple.
dateNote: From the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile, 593 BC (Ezekiel 1:2), to his last dated message in the twenty-seventh year, 571 BC (Ezekiel 29:17).

title: Nebuchadnezzar humbled
summary: Daniel warns Nebuchadnezzar that a dream of a great tree cut down is about him. A year later, boasting over Babylon, the king is driven out to live like an animal until he acknowledges that God rules. Restored, he praises "the King of heaven": "He is able to humble those who walk in pride."
dateNote: Scripture doesn't date it; it's placed late in his reign (605–562 BC), after his great building in Babylon (Daniel 4:30).

title: Daniel's visions
summary: Daniel sees four great beasts rise from the sea and "One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven," given a kingdom "that will never be destroyed"; a ram and a goat; seventy weeks decreed for his people; and wars between the kings of the north and the south. He is told to "seal the book until the time of the end."
dateNote: Dated by when Daniel saw them, not by what they foretell: from the first year of Belshazzar, about 553 BC (Daniel 7:1), to the third year of Cyrus, 536 BC (Daniel 10:1).

title: Babylon falls to Persia
summary: As Belshazzar feasts, a hand writes on the wall and Daniel reads its judgment. That night Babylon falls to the armies of Cyrus.
dateNote: The Nabonidus Chronicle records the city's fall on 16 Tashritu, 12 October 539 BC.

title: Daniel in the lions' den
summary: Daniel keeps praying to God despite the king's decree, is thrown to the lions, and is kept safe.
dateNote: Under "Darius the Mede," soon after Babylon fell (Daniel 6). Who Darius was is debated; he may be Cyrus's governor Gubaru, or Cyrus himself.

title: Cyrus lets the exiles return
summary: In his first year Cyrus decrees that the Jews may go home and rebuild the temple, and returns its gold and silver vessels.
dateNote: Cyrus's first year in Babylon, 538 BC (Ezra 1:1). The Cyrus Cylinder records his policy of returning captive peoples and their gods to their homes.

title: The first exiles return
summary: About fifty thousand exiles return with Zerubbabel, rebuild the altar, and lay the foundation of the new temple amid shouts and weeping. When they turn away the people of the land who offer to help, their neighbors frighten the builders and hire counselors against them, and the work stops until Darius's day.
dateNote: The temple's foundation was laid in the second month of the second year after their return (Ezra 3:8).

title: The second temple completed
summary: After years of opposition and neglect, Haggai and Zechariah stir the people to build, and the temple is finished and dedicated.
dateNote: Work resumed in Darius's second year, 520 BC (Haggai 1:15), and the temple was finished on 3 Adar in his sixth year, March 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).

title: Zechariah's visions
summary: While the temple is being rebuilt, Zechariah sees eight visions in one night: horsemen among the myrtles, a lampstand fed by two olive trees, a flying scroll. To Zerubbabel he says, "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts." Later oracles look ahead to Zion's King, "humble and riding on a donkey," and to the day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.
dateNote: From the eighth month of Darius's second year, 520 BC (Zechariah 1:1), to the fourth of the ninth month of his fourth year, December 518 BC (Zechariah 7:1). Chapters 9–14 aren't dated; some place them later in Zechariah's life.

title: The battle of Marathon
summary: Athens defeats Darius I's invading army at Marathon. Persia's wars with Greece go on under Xerxes, the Ahasuerus of Esther.
dateNote: 490 BC, told by the Greek historian Herodotus.

title: Esther saves her people
summary: When Queen Vashti refuses King Ahasuerus, the young Jewish woman Esther is made queen in her place. Haman plots to destroy the Jews of the Persian Empire, and Esther's cousin Mordecai urges her: "who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" She risks her life to plead with the king, and the day set for their destruction becomes a day of deliverance, remembered at Purim.
dateNote: The lots were cast in Ahasuerus's twelfth year (Esther 3:7). He is usually identified with Xerxes I, which places the day in March 473 BC.

title: Ezra returns to Jerusalem
summary: Ezra the scribe leads a second group home with the king's blessing, to teach God's Law in Judah. Finding that many, leaders among them, have married women of the surrounding peoples, he weeps and confesses before the house of God, and the people agree to send the foreign wives away.
dateNote: In Artaxerxes's seventh year, 458 BC (Ezra 7:7–9).

title: The book of Psalms gathered
summary: Psalms written over nine centuries, by Moses, David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and others, are gathered into one book in five parts: the Psalter Jesus and his first followers knew.
dateNote: Not dated. The latest psalms come from the exile and the return (Psalms 126 and 137), so the book was completed after them; many link its final form with the time of Ezra.

title: Joel and the locusts
summary: After a plague of locusts strips the land, Joel calls priests and people to fast and return to the Lord, warns of the day of the Lord, and promises that God will pour out his Spirit on all people, words Peter quotes at Pentecost.
dateNote: Joel names no king. Most now place him after the return, about 450–430 BC, before Malachi (some later still): the temple stands, elders and priests lead, and Judah's people have been scattered and sold to the Greeks (Joel 3:2, 6). Many others place him about 835 BC, while the priest Jehoiada ruled for the boy-king Joash, where his place among the early prophets suggests. Scripture doesn't say how long he prophesied.

title: Nehemiah rebuilds the walls
summary: Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, returns as governor. Despite threats from enemies the people rebuild Jerusalem's walls in fifty-two days, then hear Ezra read the Law: "the joy of the LORD is your strength." They confess their sins, sign a covenant to keep the Law, and dedicate the walls with two great choirs.
dateNote: Nehemiah went to the king in Artaxerxes's twentieth year, 445 BC (Nehemiah 2:1); the wall took fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15).

title: Malachi, the last prophet
summary: Back in Jerusalem for a second term, Nehemiah finds the temple neglected, the Sabbath broken and marriages to foreign women again. Malachi rebukes the same careless worship and broken marriages, and promises that the Lord will send Elijah before he comes. Then Scripture falls silent for four hundred years.
dateNote: Not dated. Malachi faces the same problems Nehemiah did on his return after Artaxerxes's thirty-second year, 433 BC (Nehemiah 13:6), so he is usually placed about 430 BC.

title: Alexander the Great conquers Persia
summary: Alexander of Macedon sweeps through the Persian Empire, taking Tyre and then Judea. Greek becomes the common language of the east, the language the New Testament will be written in.
dateNote: History, not Scripture: Alexander took Tyre after a seven-month siege in 332 BC. Many readers see him in Daniel's vision of a swift goat from the west (Daniel 8:5–8, 21).

title: The Septuagint
summary: Jewish scholars in Alexandria translate the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek. The apostles often quote this translation.
dateNote: The Torah was translated in the third century BC, by tradition under Ptolemy II; the other books followed over the next century or so.

title: Antiochus IV desecrates the temple
summary: Antiochus IV outlaws the Sabbath and circumcision and sets up an altar to Zeus in the temple, sacrificing on it. Faithful Jews resist, and the Maccabees take up arms.
dateNote: December 167 BC, told in 1 Maccabees 1. Many readers see it in Daniel's "abomination of desolation" (Daniel 11:31).

title: The Maccabees rededicate the temple
summary: After Antiochus IV defiles the temple and outlaws Judaism, Judas Maccabeus leads a revolt, retakes Jerusalem and rededicates the temple. Jews remember it at Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication Jesus kept (John 10:22).
dateNote: History, not Scripture (except as Catholic and Orthodox Christians count 1 Maccabees): told in 1 Maccabees 4 and by Josephus, in December 164 BC.

title: Rome takes Jerusalem
summary: The Roman general Pompey captures Jerusalem and enters the temple. Judea comes under Roman rule.
dateNote: History, not Scripture: recorded by Josephus, in 63 BC.

title: Julius Caesar assassinated
summary: Senators kill Julius Caesar in Rome. The civil wars that follow end with his heir Octavian as Augustus, Rome's first emperor.
dateNote: The Ides of March, 44 BC.

title: Herod the Great's reign
summary: Rome makes Herod king of Judea. He rules ruthlessly, builds fortresses and cities, and rebuilds the temple on a grand scale.
dateNote: From his capture of Jerusalem in 37 BC to his death in 4 BC, by Josephus's account. The temple's rebuilding began about 20 BC; John 2:20 says it had been under way for forty-six years.

title: Birth of Jesus
summary: Joseph and Mary travel to Bethlehem for a Roman census, and Jesus is born there. Angels announce him to shepherds, and magi from the east come to worship.
dateNote: Before Herod the Great died in 4 BC (Matthew 2:1, 19), probably about 6–4 BC. Scripture doesn't give the day.

title: The boy Jesus in the temple
summary: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem after Passover, listening to the teachers and asking them questions: "Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?"

title: Jesus' ministry
summary: Jesus calls disciples, preaches the kingdom of God, heals the sick and forgives sinners, mostly around the Sea of Galilee, going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.
dateNote: John's Gospel names at least three Passovers (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55), so about three years. The crucifixion is dated AD 30 here, when 14 Nisan fell on Friday 7 April; AD 33 (3 April) is the main alternative.

title: Jesus is baptized
summary: John baptizes Jesus in the Jordan. The Spirit descends like a dove and a voice from heaven says, "You are My beloved Son."
dateNote: John began preaching in the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1), AD 26–29 depending on how his reign is counted; Jesus was "about thirty" (Luke 3:23).

title: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness
summary: The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days, where he answers each of the devil's temptations with Scripture.

title: Water into wine at Cana
summary: At a wedding, when the wine runs out, Jesus turns water into wine, the first of his signs, and his disciples believe in him.

title: Jesus and Nicodemus
summary: A Pharisee comes to Jesus by night and hears that he must be born again: "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son."
dateNote: At Jesus' first Passover in Jerusalem (John 2:13, 23).

title: The woman at the well
summary: Passing through Samaria, Jesus offers a Samaritan woman living water and tells her he is the Messiah. Many in her town believe.

title: Jesus calls fishermen
summary: By the Sea of Galilee Jesus calls Simon and Andrew, James and John from their nets: "Come, follow Me," he says, "and I will make you fishers of men."
dateNote: After John the Baptist was arrested, when Jesus began preaching in Galilee (Mark 1:14).

title: The Sermon on the Mount
summary: On a hillside in Galilee Jesus teaches the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, and what life in God's kingdom looks like.
dateNote: Not dated; early in the Galilean ministry. Tradition places it on a hill above Capernaum.

title: Jesus calms the storm
summary: A storm swamps the disciples' boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind, and the sea becomes calm: "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?"

title: Feeding the five thousand
summary: Jesus feeds a crowd of five thousand men, besides women and children, with five loaves and two fish. The only miracle all four Gospels record.
dateNote: "Now the Jewish Feast of the Passover was near" (John 6:4).

title: Jesus walks on the water
summary: The night after feeding the crowd, Jesus comes to his disciples walking on the sea. Peter steps out to meet him, and begins to sink.

title: Peter's confession
summary: "Who do you say I am?" Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." From then on Jesus tells them he must suffer, die and rise.

title: The transfiguration
summary: On a high mountain Jesus' face shines like the sun; Moses and Elijah appear with him, and a voice says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!"
dateNote: Six days after Peter's confession (Matthew 17:1). Tradition places it on Mount Tabor; many prefer Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi.

title: Jesus raises Lazarus
summary: Four days after Lazarus is buried, Jesus calls him out of the tomb: "I am the resurrection and the life." The leaders resolve to kill Jesus.
dateNote: Shortly before Jesus' last Passover (John 11:55).

title: Zacchaeus
summary: On his last journey to Jerusalem, Jesus calls a chief tax collector down from a sycamore tree in Jericho and goes to his house. "Today salvation has come to this house."

title: Jesus enters Jerusalem
summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey as crowds wave palm branches and shout "Hosanna!"
dateNote: The day after he came to Bethany, six days before Passover (John 12:1, 12). The crucifixion is dated AD 30 here, when 14 Nisan fell on Friday 7 April; AD 33 (3 April) is the main alternative.

title: Jesus clears the temple
summary: Jesus drives out the money-changers and sellers: "My house will be called a house of prayer. But you are making it 'a den of robbers.'"
dateNote: The day after the entry into Jerusalem (Mark 11:12–15). John tells of a temple cleansing early in the ministry (John 2:13–17).

title: The Last Supper
summary: Jesus shares a final meal with his disciples, gives them bread and wine as his body and blood of the new covenant, then prays in Gethsemane, where he is arrested.
dateNote: The crucifixion is dated AD 30 here, when 14 Nisan fell on Friday 7 April; AD 33 (3 April) is the main alternative.

title: The crucifixion
summary: After trials before the high priest and Pilate, Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two criminals, and dies. He is buried in a nearby tomb.
dateNote: On the day of Preparation for the Passover (John 19:14, 31). The crucifixion is dated AD 30 here, when 14 Nisan fell on Friday 7 April; AD 33 (3 April) is the main alternative.

title: The resurrection
summary: On the third day the tomb is empty. Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, to Peter, to the disciples, and to more than five hundred others.
dateNote: The crucifixion is dated AD 30 here, when 14 Nisan fell on Friday 7 April; AD 33 (3 April) is the main alternative.

title: The road to Emmaus
summary: The risen Jesus walks with two disciples, explaining from the Scriptures why the Christ had to suffer; they recognize him as he breaks the bread.

title: Breakfast by the sea
summary: In Galilee the risen Jesus gives the fishing disciples a great catch and cooks them breakfast. Three times he asks Peter, "Do you love Me?" and tells him, "Feed My sheep."
dateNote: Between the resurrection and the ascension.

title: The ascension
summary: Forty days after rising, Jesus sends his disciples to be his witnesses to the ends of the earth, and is taken up into heaven from the Mount of Olives.
dateNote: Acts 1:3. Luke places it near Bethany, on the Mount of Olives (Luke 24:50; Acts 1:12).

title: Pentecost
summary: The Holy Spirit comes on the disciples with wind and fire, and they speak in other languages. Peter preaches, and about three thousand are baptized.
dateNote: Fifty days after the resurrection (Acts 2:1).

title: A lame man healed at the temple
summary: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!" Peter and John heal a man lame from birth, preach to the crowd, and are arrested and warned by the council.
dateNote: Not dated; soon after Pentecost.

title: Stephen is stoned
summary: Stephen is stoned after his defense before the council, with a young man named Saul approving. Persecution scatters the believers beyond Jerusalem.
dateNote: Not dated; a short time after Pentecost and before Paul's conversion.

title: Philip and the Ethiopian
summary: Scattered by persecution, Philip preaches in Samaria, then on the desert road to Gaza explains Isaiah to an Ethiopian official, who believes and is baptized.

title: Paul meets Jesus on the road to Damascus
summary: On his way to arrest believers in Damascus, Saul is blinded by a light from heaven and hears the risen Jesus. He is baptized and begins to preach Christ.
dateNote: Paul counts three years and then fourteen years to his visits to Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18; 2:1), placing his conversion about AD 31–33.

title: Peter and Cornelius
summary: A vision teaches Peter not to call any person unclean. He preaches to the Roman centurion Cornelius, and the Spirit falls on Gentiles for the first time.
dateNote: Not dated; between Paul's conversion and Herod Agrippa I's death in AD 44 (Acts 12).

title: Paul's first missionary journey
summary: Sent out by the church at Antioch, Paul and Barnabas preach through Cyprus and the cities of southern Galatia, then return strengthening the new churches.
dateNote: Before the Jerusalem council of about AD 49.

title: The council at Jerusalem
summary: The apostles and elders decide that Gentile believers don't need to be circumcised or keep the Law of Moses to be saved.

title: Paul's second missionary journey
summary: Paul and Silas revisit Galatia, then cross into Europe at God's call: Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, and eighteen months in Corinth.
dateNote: Paul's time in Corinth overlaps Gallio's term as proconsul (Acts 18:12), which an inscription at Delphi dates to AD 51–52.

title: Paul's third missionary journey
summary: Paul spends over two years teaching in Ephesus, where the gospel spreads through all Asia, then visits the churches of Macedonia and Greece.

title: Paul writes to the Romans
summary: From Corinth Paul writes his fullest account of the gospel to the church in Rome, which he hopes to visit on his way to Spain.
dateNote: Written during his three months in Greece, as he prepared to take a gift to Jerusalem (Acts 20:2–3; Romans 15:25–26).

title: Paul arrested in Jerusalem
summary: A riot breaks out when Paul visits the temple. Roman soldiers take him into custody, and he is held at Caesarea for two years.
dateNote: Paul hurried to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (Acts 20:16).

title: Paul's voyage to Rome
summary: Having appealed to Caesar, Paul sails for Rome under guard. The ship is wrecked on Malta, and he reaches Rome the next spring.
dateNote: Festus took over from Felix about AD 59 (Acts 24:27). They sailed after the autumn fast and wintered three months on Malta (Acts 27:9; 28:11).

title: Paul's letters from prison
summary: Under house arrest in Rome, Paul welcomes visitors and writes to the Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon.
dateNote: Two years in Rome (Acts 28:30). Some place one or more of these letters earlier, in Ephesus or Caesarea.

title: Paul's last letter
summary: Imprisoned again in Rome and expecting to die, Paul writes to Timothy: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith."
dateNote: Tradition says Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero, about AD 64–67, and that Peter was crucified there too.

title: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
summary: Rome crushes a Jewish revolt. Titus's army takes Jerusalem and burns the temple, as Jesus had foretold.
dateNote: History, not narrated in Scripture: Josephus describes the siege and the burning of the temple in August AD 70. Jesus foretold it (Luke 21:20–24).

title: John's vision on Patmos
summary: Exiled on Patmos, John sees the risen Christ, receives letters for seven churches of Asia, and is shown the defeat of evil and the new heaven and new earth.
dateNote: Irenaeus (about AD 180) places John's vision late in Domitian's reign, about AD 95; some date it before AD 70, under Nero. The visions themselves aren't events in time and aren't placed on the timeline.

title: Paul stoned at Lystra
summary: Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd hails Paul and Barnabas as Zeus and Hermes. Then opponents turn the crowd, and Paul is stoned and left for dead, but gets up and goes back into the city.

title: Paul and Silas in prison at Philippi
summary: Lydia believes and opens her home. Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed; at midnight, as they sing hymns, an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer and his household believe.

title: Paul at the Areopagus
summary: Troubled by the idols of Athens, Paul tells its philosophers about their altar "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD" and the God who made the world and raised Jesus from the dead.

title: The riot at Ephesus
summary: So many turn from idols that the silversmiths who make shrines of Artemis stir up the city. A mob fills the theater shouting "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" for two hours.

title: Eutychus raised at Troas
summary: As Paul talks late into the night, a young man falls asleep and drops from a third-floor window. Paul embraces him, and he is alive.
dateNote: They sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and reached Troas five days later (Acts 20:6).

title: Farewell to the Ephesian elders
summary: At Miletus Paul calls the elders of Ephesus, charges them to shepherd God's flock, and tells them they will not see him again. They kneel, pray and weep together.

title: Shipwreck on Malta
summary: A storm drives the ship for fourteen days until it runs aground off Malta; all 276 aboard reach land. A viper bites Paul without harming him, and he heals the sick of the island.
dateNote: Some two weeks after leaving Crete late in the sailing season (Acts 27:9, 27).

title: The flight to Egypt
summary: Warned in a dream that Herod will seek the child's life, Joseph takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt by night. After Herod dies they return and settle in Nazareth.
dateNote: Soon after the magi's visit; they stayed until Herod died in 4 BC (Matthew 2:15, 19).

title: The angel comes to Mary
summary: Gabriel tells Mary, a virgin engaged to Joseph, that she will bear the Son of God. "May it happen to me according to your word." She visits her relative Elizabeth, who is expecting John.
dateNote: About nine months before Jesus' birth, probably about 6–5 BC.

title: Believers first called Christians
summary: Believers from Cyprus and Cyrene preach to Greeks in Antioch, and many turn to the Lord. Barnabas brings Saul from Tarsus to teach there for a year.
dateNote: The year before the famine relief visit and Herod Agrippa I's death in AD 44 (Acts 11:27–30; 12:23).

title: Peter freed from prison
summary: Herod Agrippa kills James the brother of John and jails Peter. While the church prays, an angel leads Peter out past the guards.
dateNote: Shortly before Herod Agrippa I died in AD 44 (Acts 12:20–23), a death Josephus also records.

title: The letter of James
summary: James, leader of the Jerusalem church, writes to believers scattered abroad: faith without works is dead.
dateNote: Often dated before AD 50, which would make it one of the earliest New Testament books; others date it near James's death in AD 62.

title: Paul writes to the Galatians
summary: Paul warns the Galatian churches against those who say Gentiles must keep the Law: a person is justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the Law.
dateNote: If written to the churches of the first journey before the Jerusalem council, about AD 48 from Antioch; others date it AD 53–55, from Ephesus.

title: Paul writes to the Thessalonians
summary: From Corinth, after Timothy brings news of their faith under persecution, Paul writes two letters to encourage the young church and teach about the Lord's return.
dateNote: Written soon after Paul reached Corinth (1 Thessalonians 3:6; Acts 18:5).

title: Paul writes 1 Corinthians
summary: From Ephesus Paul answers the divided church in Corinth: on factions, marriage, worship, the gifts of the Spirit, love, and the resurrection.
dateNote: Written at Ephesus before Pentecost (1 Corinthians 16:8).

title: Paul writes 2 Corinthians
summary: Relieved by Titus's news, Paul writes from Macedonia about his trials, the ministry of the new covenant, and God's power made perfect in weakness.
dateNote: Written in Macedonia after leaving Ephesus (2 Corinthians 2:12–13; 7:5–7), perhaps at Philippi.

title: Mark's Gospel
summary: Mark writes the shortest and probably earliest Gospel, a fast-moving account of Jesus the Son of God, who came to serve and give his life.
dateNote: Early tradition (Papias, Irenaeus) says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching, probably in Rome. Dates proposed range from the 50s to about AD 70.

title: Luke writes his Gospel and Acts
summary: Luke, after carefully investigating everything, writes an orderly account for Theophilus: Jesus' life, then the spread of the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome.
dateNote: Acts ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome, about AD 62, so many date it then, with the Gospel a little earlier. Others date both to the 70s or 80s.

title: Peter's letters
summary: Writing from "Babylon" (likely Rome), Peter encourages suffering believers across Asia Minor to stand firm in grace, and warns against false teachers.
dateNote: Before his death under Nero, which tradition places in Rome about AD 64–67 (1 Peter 5:13; 2 Peter 1:14).

title: The letter of Jude
summary: Jude, brother of James, urges believers to contend for the faith against false teachers who turn grace into a license for immorality, and closes with a doxology to the one able to keep them from stumbling.
dateNote: Not dated; usually placed AD 60–80. Much of it is shared with 2 Peter 2. Where it was written isn't known.

title: Paul writes to Timothy and Titus
summary: Paul instructs his co-workers Timothy in Ephesus and Titus on Crete in choosing leaders, guarding sound teaching and caring for the church.
dateNote: Probably between Paul's two Roman imprisonments, years that Acts doesn't cover.

title: The great fire of Rome
summary: Fire destroys much of Rome. Nero blames the Christians and has many put to death, the first persecution by Rome; tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul under Nero.
dateNote: July AD 64, told by the Roman historian Tacitus.

title: Matthew's Gospel
summary: Matthew presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets, gathering his teaching into five great discourses.
dateNote: Usually dated between the 50s and the 80s; where it was written isn't known. Tradition says Matthew wrote first, for Jewish believers.

title: The Jewish revolt
summary: Judea rises against Rome. Vespasian and then his son Titus crush the revolt, taking Jerusalem in AD 70 and Masada a few years later.
dateNote: AD 66–73 (or 74, when Masada fell), told by Josephus, who fought in it.

title: The letter to the Hebrews
summary: An unnamed teacher urges Jewish believers tempted to turn back not to drift away: Jesus is the great high priest and the final sacrifice, better than all that came before.
dateNote: Its author isn't named. It speaks of the temple's sacrifices as still going on (Hebrews 10:1–3), so it's usually dated before AD 70.

title: John's Gospel and letters
summary: Late in life John writes "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God," and three letters calling believers to walk in the light and love one another.
dateNote: Irenaeus says John wrote at Ephesus late in life, about AD 85–95. Some date the Gospel earlier.
